name: SUNCT/SUNA
aliases: short-lasting unilateral neuralgiform headache attacks with conjunctival injection and tearing

reference.source: ICHD-3 / International Classification of Sleep Disorders
clinicalPearls: Short-lasting unilateral neuralgiform headache attacks lasting seconds to a few minutes and recurring many times an hour
SUNCT requires both conjunctival injection and tearing; SUNA has only one of these, or neither
The attacks are among the most frequent of all headaches, sometimes dozens or more per hour
Cutaneous or movement triggers can provoke attacks, overlapping with trigeminal neuralgia, but the autonomic features are prominent and there is typically no refractory period
The disorder is poorly responsive to indometacin, which helps separate it from paroxysmal hemicrania
Lamotrigine is often the preferred preventive, and intravenous lidocaine can help settle severe bouts
MRI, including views of the posterior fossa and pituitary, is important because symptomatic cases occur, sometimes from neurovascular contact with the trigeminal nerve
reference.pathophysiology: SUNCT and SUNA are trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias in which very brief paroxysms arise from trigeminovascular activation coupled to a cranial parasympathetic reflex, producing the ipsilateral autonomic signs. Posterior hypothalamic activation is seen on functional imaging, and neurovascular compression of the trigeminal nerve is identified in a proportion of cases, giving clinical overlap with trigeminal neuralgia.
additionalDifferentials: Symptomatic trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia from a posterior fossa or pituitary lesion
additionalInvestigations: Detailed characterisation of attack duration, frequency, triggers and autonomic features
MRI brain with dedicated pituitary and posterior fossa imaging and vascular sequences
Assessment for neurovascular contact of the trigeminal nerve
Trial of indometacin to help exclude paroxysmal hemicrania
Review for cutaneous trigger zones and the presence or absence of a refractory period
redFlags: Abnormal neurological signs or an underlying structural lesion on imaging
First presentation in older age or rapidly escalating attacks
Attacks that do not fit the expected very-short, very-frequent profile
reference.prognosis: The course is variable, ranging from single bouts to a chronic unremitting pattern; many patients improve with preventive drugs such as lamotrigine, and identifying a symptomatic cause can allow targeted treatment.
pitfalls: Confusing the disorder with trigeminal neuralgia and missing the prominent autonomic features
Expecting an indometacin response as seen in paroxysmal hemicrania
Omitting MRI and overlooking a symptomatic lesion or neurovascular contact
Escalating opioids for what is a neuralgiform, opioid-unresponsive disorder
references: International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd edition (ICHD-3)
management: Start lamotrigine as the preferred preventive to reduce attack frequency
Use alternative preventives such as topiramate, gabapentin or oxcarbazepine when lamotrigine is ineffective or not tolerated
Settle severe exacerbations with intravenous lidocaine as a transitional measure
Arrange MRI to identify a symptomatic cause and treat any pituitary or posterior fossa lesion found
Consider microvascular decompression where trigeminal neurovascular contact is demonstrated, or neuromodulation such as occipital nerve stimulation in refractory cases
Refer to a specialist headache service for diagnosis and management of refractory disease
